Roles of peripheral myeloid cells in Alzheimer disease (AD)

a, Monocytes and/or macrophages and Aβ. Peripheral monocytes and/or macrophages can sense and engulf amyoid-β (Aβ). The endogenous cysteine protease inhibitor CST7108 and the receptor CD36107 have been linked with inhibiting Aβ phagocytosis, while formyl peptide receptor-like-1 (FPRL1) and formyl peptide receptor 2 (FPR2)104,105, toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2)96 have been linked with promoting Aβ phagocytosis in monocytes and/or macrophages. Several key AD GWAS genes, including those encoding CD33245, triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2)101, TREM1102 and leukocyte immunoglobulin-like receptor subfamily B member 2 (LILRB2)100, modulate this phagocytic ability. AD gene risk mutations in TREM1102, TREM2 101 and the AD risk allele APOE4 have been reported to inhibit phagocytosis99. It has been reported that peripheral monocytes show accelerated chemotraction to Aβ compared to microglia86 and that CCR2+ monocytes are the primary immune cells from the periphery recognising amyloid-β compared to neutrophils or lymphocytes89. However, with aging and AD progression monocytes undergo apoptosis more quickly at the brain border 95–98. In human APOE 4 carriers, monocyte and/or macrophage phagocytic capacity is reduced compared to APOE3 carriers99. b, Recruitment and roles of brain border-associated macrophages (BAMs) in AD. In AD models, C-C chemokine receptor type 2 (CCR2) is crucial for the recruitment of monocytes and macrophages to the brain and loss of this protein worsens pathology126. Parenchymal border macrophages (a type of BAM found in the meninges and/or vasculature) regulate CSF flow98; their loss causes debris buildup, high interferon-γ (IFN-γ) in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and faster AD pathology progression. Expression of APOE4 in BAMs leads to reactive oxygen species (ROS)-mediated vascular damage and cognitive decline127 and replacing APOE4 BAMs with APOE3 BAMs is protective 127. c, Neutrophils and AD. Neutrophils infiltrate the brain via integrin alpha-L (LFA-1; blockade of LFA-1 is beneficial)129. Neutrophils adhering to blood vessels reduce blood flow; removing them improves perfusion134. Female APOE4 carriers with AD have neutrophils secreting high levels of interleukin 17F (IL-17F), which impairs cognition50. Neutrophil IL-17F signals to microglia (via IL-17RA), inducing a damaging loop that involves interleukin 1α (IL-1α), interleukin-18 (IL-18) and tumour necrosis factor (TNF); blocking this pathway or removing APOE4 from neutrophils restores microglial function50. APOE4 neutrophils also produce more NETs including MPO50. Chronic neutrophil activation leads to an immunosuppressive phenotype (indicated by checkpoint signalling and degranulation gene upregulation) as seen in AD (exhaustion), and accumulation of toxic monocyte signatures correlates with cognitive decline in AD133
